headline: Pulao rice price doubles in 6 months, farmers miss out on profits as stock runs dry
summary: The price of Pulao rice has surged by 100% in just six months, reaching unprecedented levels, while farmers who sold their paddy earlier are not benefiting from the current market boom.
details: In Rajshahi, the price of Pulao rice has doubled in the last six months, with traders reporting they have never seen such a drastic increase. A kilogram of rice that cost BDT 100 is now selling for BDT 200-230.
Farmers, however, did not benefit from this surge. They sold their paddy at much lower prices during the harvest season, and by the time prices started climbing, their stock was already depleted.
Many farmers and traders attribute the price hike to the export of Pulao rice. In the 2025-26 fiscal year, three leading companies collectively exported 1,530 metric tons of rice.

Pulao rice is primarily made from BRRI-34 (Chinigura) paddy, mostly cultivated in Dinajpur, with some production in Thakurgaon and Panchagarh. Dinajpur aimed to produce paddy on 260,860 hectares this year, including 95,000 hectares for Chinigura.
Major companies like Square Food & Beverage, Ispahani Agro, and Pran Agro package and market this fragrant rice. However, farmers did not receive the current high prices for their produce.

Consumers express shock at the sudden price jump. One buyer in Rajshahi found the price jumped from BDT 140 to BDT 230 per kg in five months, questioning why prices would rise so sharply due to exports.

Restaurant owners are also struggling, buying rice at BDT 200 per kg compared to BDT 130 six months ago, but unable to increase their menu prices proportionally. Wholesale prices range from BDT 180-200 per kg, with higher retail prices.

The National Consumer Rights Protection Directorate has taken action, fining a Rajshahi wholesaler BDT 10,000 for selling Pulao rice at BDT 200 per kg. The wholesaler argued they bought it from company warehouses at similar high prices.

Farmers like Khaledul Islam from Parbatipur, Dinajpur, sold a 75 kg sack of Chinigura paddy for BDT 4,000-5,200 last season. By the time prices rose to BDT 5,200, their stock was gone, preventing them from profiting from the higher market rates.

headline: Four of six Citizen Service Centers locked in Dhaka; project launched by interim government stalls
summary: The centers, meant to offer 450 government services like passports and NID, are largely non-operational due to lack of equipment and support, frustrating entrepreneurs who joined the initiative.
details: Six Citizen Service Centers, including one in Mohammadpur, launched by the special assistant to the chief advisor of the previous interim government, are largely non-functional. Four of these centers are currently locked, with no service providers or recipients present.

A visit to the Mohammadpur center on August 27 revealed an empty room with disarranged tables and chairs. Entrepreneurs were meant to offer around 450 government services like passports, NID, and birth registration, earning a fixed fee.

Md. Mustakim, Mohammadpur's entrepreneur, left his computer service business for this initiative but received no promised equipment from the ICT division. With no service seekers, he no longer visits the center, mirroring the fate of many others.

A wider investigation confirmed that four of the six pilot project centers are locked, while the remaining two are only occasionally open and at risk of closing. Entrepreneurs like Rajit Khan from Nilkhet and Ashikur Rahman from Uttara also reported a lack of essential equipment and support, forcing them to seek other work.

The centers were launched on May 26 with the slogan 'all citizen services at one address', inaugurated by Professor Muhammad Yunus, then Chief Advisor of the interim government. The stated goal was to reduce middlemen and ensure hassle-free services.

However, the interim government failed to ensure necessary internet connectivity, computers, printers, biometric devices, or effective links with government portals. An anonymous ICT official called the initiative superficial, lacking a dedicated budget and proper promotion.

Entrepreneurs complained about the lack of government-provided internet and their inability to secure connections without formal contracts. Despite not being officially closed by the current government, the Citizen Service initiative's centers remain largely non-functional.
